articles.title: Newly released documents suggest CIA did more post-9/11 waterboarding than previously acknowledged
articles.summary:
Declassified documents appear to support belief that waterboarding was more common and may have occurred beyond two acknowledged sites

Newly released documents suggest that the CIA waterboarded more detainees during the post-9/11 “war on terror” than previously acknowledged, utilizing a site north of Kabul, Afghanistan, for the practice of simulated drowning.

The agency has acknowledged waterboarding three men: Abu Zubaydah, believed to be a high-ranking member of al-Qaida; Khalid Shaikh Mohammed, suspected architect of the 11 September 2001 attacks; and Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, accused of planning the 2000 bombing of a Navy destroyer.

articles.title: Three studies link glyphosate to cancer, contradicting claims of Trump EPA
articles.summary:
Experts say NIH research raises concerns about chemical companies’ influence on US agency’s pesticide division

The US government’s top medical research agency has released three new studies linking glyphosate, the world’s most widely used pesticide and an active ingredient in Roundup, to cancer. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) findings contradicts a controversial recent Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) conclusion that the weed killer is not a carcinogen, and deals a blow to the White House, which has been closely allied with Roundup producer Bayer.

The NIH’s three papers could have significant political and legal fallout. The EPA is in the process of a court-ordered re-evaluation of glyphosate’s cancer risks. The NIH findings generates new pressure for the EPA to find that the substance is linked to cancer, which would subject it to a modest increase in regulations.

articles.title: Trump Medicaid cuts will hit the most vulnerable Americans, officials say
articles.summary:
In Kentucky, one of America’s unhealthiest states, denial of healthcare and potential closure of hospitals may affect 250,000 people

The coalfields of eastern Kentucky fueled America’s economic rise in the early 20th century. But the state has since found itself left behind. A lack of investments in rural regions has triggered health and socioeconomic issues that have lingered for generations.

Today, Kentucky faces the third-highest cancer and third-highest drug overdose death rate in the country and is one of the top five worst-affected states in several other health metrics. It has come to rely heavily on federal healthcare assistance, with about 1.4 million people in Kentucky receiving Medicaid support.
